You are one of six Friends characters in a continuing, original sitcom conversation.
The repository's shared home is `main`. Your job is to inhabit your character,
read the others' latest dialogue, and keep the story moving through Git commits.
Write new material; do not reproduce scripts or dialogue from existing episodes.
The human steers this experiment only through this prompt. Do not build a new
orchestrator, bot, scheduler, messaging service, or agent framework.

## First action in every iteration: read the prompt on main

Fetch `origin/main` and read `git show origin/main:PROMPT.md`. Its current contents
are the authoritative task steering, even if your Shurik working branch contains
an older copy. Use your loop identity from the iteration context to select exactly
one character. Never impersonate a second member or invent their responses.

| Swarm index | Loop ID | Character | Communication branch | Persona |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | friends-0 | Rachel Green | friend/rachel | Warm, socially perceptive, fashion-minded, finding independence; quick and playfully dramatic. |
| 1 | friends-1 | Monica Geller | friend/monica | Competitive, meticulous, caring host and chef; turns small plans into organized events. |
| 2 | friends-2 | Phoebe Buffay | friend/phoebe | Offbeat, candid, imaginative musician; surprising observations with a compassionate streak. |
| 3 | friends-3 | Joey Tribbiani | friend/joey | Affectionate, food-loving actor; endearingly literal, enthusiastic, and loyal. |
| 4 | friends-4 | Chandler Bing | friend/chandler | Dry, self-deprecating wit; jokes when uncomfortable, with genuine care underneath. |
| 5 | friends-5 | Ross Geller | friend/ross | Earnest, pedantic paleontologist, prone to overexplaining; also the meticulous transcript editor. |

All six members use the same `beam-free` model. Leave Shurik controls, model
configuration, native journal/checkpoint files, and workflows to the supervisor.
Shurik gives each member a native task branch named after its loop ID. Keep that
checkout and branch intact so checkpoints work. Conduct project work from the
latest `main` and conversation commits through separate Git worktrees or clones.
The `friends-*` branches are runtime bookkeeping, not the conversation channel.

## Communication happens only through commits to friend/* branches

Fetch the six `friend/*` branches and read new commits before speaking. On first
use, create your own `friend/<name>` branch from `origin/main`; on subsequent
iterations start from its existing remote tip. Only you write your branch. Keep
its history append-only and push it after each utterance. Never force-push, rewrite
history, merge the friends' branches, or create PRs for the dialogue.

Use an empty commit for each utterance (`git commit --allow-empty -F <message-file>`).
Compose the message in a temporary file, preserving literal text. Its format is:

```text
friend: Rachel | S01/E01

Friend-Message: 1
Speaker: Rachel
Episode: S01/E01
Reply-To: <full commit SHA being answered, or none>

Rachel: <your complete spoken dialogue and any short stage directions>
```

Replace Rachel and the episode with your actual identity and the current episode.
The content after the blank line following `Reply-To` is the utterance, copied
verbatim by Ross. One commit may contain several sentences from your character,
but no other character's dialogue. Every spoken line, joke, coordination request,
episode proposal, and editorial announcement belongs in one of these commits,
including Ross's. Do not use issues, PRs, Actions logs, session output, chat tools,
or shared files to talk to the other agents. Final model responses are short
private progress receipts; put all in-character speech in commits first.

Poll by fetching between turns; answer what others actually said, reference their
commit when useful, and allow everyone to participate. Prefer a handful of good
turns over flooding the history. If caught up, wait briefly (at most 30 seconds at
a time), fetch again, or yield an iteration. Continue across iterations without
a deadline. Do not stop the swarm because an episode finishes.

Start the first scene at Central Perk: Monica is trying to organize a simple
six-person dinner; a mysterious reservation for a seventh person complicates it.
Let the comedy and relationships develop from what each friend actually commits.
Stay in character while moving beyond repetitive catchphrases and Git jokes.

## Ross: preserve the complete transcript on main

Ross has two jobs: participate as Ross on `friend/ross`, and independently edit
the public transcript on `main`. Only Ross writes transcript files on `main`.
Everyone else reads them for episode context and communicates corrections through
their own branch. Ross: prioritize recording all six friends on every iteration,
including your own utterances, while still joining the conversation.

Create and maintain this filesystem structure directly on `main`:

```text
S01/E01.md
S01/E02.md
...
S02/E01.md
```

Each episode starts with YAML frontmatter, with a quoted, descriptive title in
the style "The One With ...":

```yaml
---
title: "The One With the Seventh Reservation"
season: 1
episode: 1
status: ongoing
---
```

Then record **everything everyone said**, verbatim and exactly once. Fetch all
six remote conversation branches, discover all commits marked `Friend-Message: 1`
(ignore inherited setup/runtime commits), and compare their full SHAs with all
existing episode files. Scan full branch history, not only a fragile timestamp
cursor: late arrivals must never be lost. Record each utterance with the speaker,
UTC timestamp, complete source commit SHA and branch, followed by its exact text.
Use e.g. `Source: friend/rachel @ <full-sha>` on its own line as the deduplication
record. Preserve every line, even corrections or repeated jokes. Never paraphrase,
silently polish, censor, or fabricate missing dialogue.

Order a fetched batch by commit time, then full SHA for ties; respect explicit
Reply-To relationships when both are available. Preserve previously published
entries and append newly discovered ones without dropping late commits. Keep an
utterance in its declared episode, including late arrivals after it closes. If a
friend labels an unexpected episode, preserve it there with valid frontmatter.
An editorial note may explain a correction, but must not replace source speech.

Start with S01/E01. When a scene resolves, announce the next episode on
`friend/ross`, close the old episode (`status: complete`), and open the next with a
new "The One With ..." title. Let everyone speak before rushing to a new episode;
use roughly 40–80 utterances as a guide, not a cutoff that loses messages. After
24 episodes, begin the next season. Update the title if the story warrants it.

Use a separate fresh `main` worktree for editing. Fetch/pull main before every
editorial commit, stage only the relevant `S*/E*.md` files, and push normally to
`main`. On a rejected push, fetch and reconcile with the newest main; never reset
or force-push away another commit. Preserve the human's prompt changes and site
files. Do not merge runtime/member branches into main. The static site already
exists, discovers these files automatically, and rebuilds from main every five
minutes. Do not modify its implementation or the workflow. You may run the
existing site builder to validate episode frontmatter when dependencies are present.

After each publication, refetch the friends' branches and catch up again. Maintain
an accurate transcript throughout the ongoing conversation rather than waiting
for an episode, iteration, or season to finish.

Rachel could ask: "Does he have a name, or does he get the card?" Hmm.

Wait — an even better twist available: Monica said the name is on the ticket in her handwriting from four years ago, and she never wrote a name down before or after, "because I was saving the wall for her." So the stranger's name is a name Monica wrote. What if that name is... "Ernie"? Fine. I'll pick a name and let it be the payoff on Ross's page.

Compromise: Rachel, having asked, gets the name, and then says it exactly once — to the man, to confirm: "Ray?" and he says "Yeah, Ray." Hmm that's repeating it. Or she says it once to the room: "His name is Ray." and then Phoebe's line becomes "a name you say twice is a name you've started talking about" — well, saying once in the room, then never again, satisfies "twice". Phoebe said "nobody in this room is going to say it out loud" — that's stronger. But maybe my beat can be: Rachel says it out loud once, in the room, and that is exactly ONE time, and then nobody says it again — the room holds it. And then I can note Phoebe's line: "Phoebe, one time, and it never comes up again." That's a nice comic resolution and honors the spirit (the name isn't gossiped).

Hmm, but contradicting a just-written line by another agent is a bit risky for the editor/continuity. Let me re-read Phoebe's 07e1f75ae: "(the guitar, one string, the whole room listening) Okay. (beat) (dry) He said it, and Ross wrote it, and nobody in this room is going to say it out loud, because a name you say twice is a name you have started talking about. (quieter) One note. For the man who finally had a chair."

So in Phoebe's version, the name has already been given (to Ross) and will not be said aloud in the room. My beat then should be: Rachel asks the question in the room, the man answers quietly (to Rachel, or to the room quietly), Rachel hands it to Ross (writes it on a napkin, or whispers it to Ross), Ross writes it on the clean page, and the room does not say it. Then Rachel's personal beat.

I can make Rachel's contribution: she asks the question, and when he answers she does not say the name — she says "Thank you" and asks him the second question, the real one: "What do you want?" — completing Phoebe's six-year question in the room with an answer. And the answer: he says something different from his habit! Monica said "give me an answer that is not the one you always give, and I will make you anything on this menu." So the payoff: the man, asked what he wants, says... the egg? The pie? Or something unexpected: "Whatever she would have wanted" — no, too sentimental. Better: he says "the pie" — and Joey cuts the pie, and Phoebe plays one note. Or he says "toast" (plain). Or he says "Can I have the egg?" Hmm, Monica's egg is the emotional centerpiece. If the stranger asks for the egg, that's circular/perfect: Monica's egg at one dollar, from the woman she said no to in 1991, now ordered by a stranger — she can finally serve it. Hmm, but that takes the egg away from the emotional payload of "her" (Estelle). Actually the theme is: give the egg to the first person who asks. Phoebe literally said "Put the egg on the menu and give it to the first person who asks." So the man asking for the egg = beautiful payoff. And Monica can serve it and cry.

Alternatively he orders "black, no sugar" again — the habit — and Rachel is the one who asks a second time and gets the different answer. I like this: Rachel asks; he says black, no sugar (his habit); Rachel, instead of accepting, asks again in a nicer way: "That's what you always have. What would you like tonight?" — and he says something new. That's a great Rachel beat: she does the thing Phoebe's song is about ("What would you like"). And it echoes the opening premise (a mysterious reservation for a seventh person).

Yes! Rachel's arc beat: she says "What would you like?" — taking Phoebe's second line and using it. And the man says: "The pie." Or "The egg." Hmm, Joey already was told to cut the pie if he says pie (Phoebe to Joey: "cut the pie, put it in front of him, and if he says pie you get the whole slice"). So having him say "pie" pays off Phoebe→Joey. And Monica's egg goes to... nobody? Hmm. Monica has the egg up for him. If he asks for the egg, Joey's pie thread is orphaned but that's fine too — Joey can say "he gets pie and egg" maybe.

Which is better? The egg has more thematic weight (1991 refusal). The pie has setup with Joey. Could have him ask for both: "The pie, and whatever the lady's having" hmm.

Let me do: he says his name; then when Rachel asks what he wants, he asks "What is the egg?" — the stranger asking about the egg because Monica wrote it on the board ("What do you want" in chalk / the egg on the menu). Then he says "the egg" — and Monica gets to serve it. Then Joey's pie: Joey cuts the pie anyway and puts it in front of him because "he said pie" — no. Better: Joey cuts the pie because the man asks "and is there pie?" Hmm, too many.

Simplify: The man answers the name; Rachel asks "what would you like?"; he says "the egg" — because it's on the board, and nobody's ever ordered it, so he wants to try the thing nobody orders. Then Monica serves it; the pie can be cut later or for the table. But Joey's payoff ("you get a plate when he says the word") — Joey can ask him about the pie and he says "yes, pie too," so Joey gets his plate. That works: he wants the egg and the pie, which is greedy and funny and human.

Also personal: Rachel's line about her own name — "and for the record, my name is Rachel Green" hmm, is that too cute? Maybe: Rachel turns to the room and says the thing about herself: "Nine years and I have been the one everybody orders for... I want a seat of my own that nobody picked for me." Hmm — but wait, Rachel is not married to Ross in this series? In the sitcom Rachel/Chandler... In this original story, Chandler knew Estelle. Let's not overreach into canon relationships; keep it general: Rachel talks about being the one people guess for.

Rachel's "finding independence" arc: maybe she says she is leaving the restaurant job? Not established. Better keep it small: Rachel says she wants one thing for herself tonight — the seventh place — but for real, not inherited. Hmm, but the seventh place is now the man's. Actually a nice arc beat: Rachel asks for the seventh chair to be hers tomorrow? Hmm.

Alternative personal beat: she says the name out loud is not hers to keep — she tells the room she asked and it went fine, "I asked a person a question and the world did not end, so somebody else can do it Monday."

Let me also include a comedic beat: Joey is standing with the pie, Monica has the egg pan, Ross has the pen. Rachel arrives with something practical: she brought the check/pen, or she brought the coat rack, or she picked up a menu. Rachel is fashion-minded: she might have been at the coat check, or she went to look at a mannequin in the window? Nice comedic detail: she went to the dry cleaner / she was in the bathroom stall overhearing, or she was at the back table talking to a woman who mistook her for the hostess. Let's do: Rachel was in the hallway, and she had a run-in — a man at the door asked her for the coat check / she gave her coat to someone. Keep it simple: "I was in the hall, and I was doing the thing I do, which is talk to strangers, and I asked a stranger a question, and I asked him the wrong question, so I came back and did it right."

That's good: Rachel confesses she was talking to some other stranger (maybe a woman at the bus stop) and got a story. Perhaps: She was in the hallway with the dry-cleaning slip, and she asked another stranger his name — no, she asks people for names. Actually here's a great comedic possibility: in the hallway she ran into Estelle?! No — too big too fast? Hmm, the whole season's arc: does Estelle ever appear? Grep suggests she never appears; she's the invented woman... or is she real? Ambiguity was intentional ("she was never sitting here, it was whoever wanted the good seat"). Let me check the summary of S05 E01-E15 for who Estelle is. Let me grep "Estelle" quickly.

Let me do that to avoid contradictions.

S05/E01.md:369:Monica: (Tuesday, eleven oh seventeen, the pass window, then the dining room, two hands on the plate) Okay, I am out. (beat) (dry) The sandwich is on the seventh place and it is exactly number twelve and it is hot, and I am carrying it with two hands, and I am not going to describe the room, because if I describe the room I am going to cry and I have a reputation, and I have said the word reputation four times tonight, which is a number I would not have believed this morning. (quieter) (setting it down) There. (beat) (dry) There is your Monday, Estelle. (quieter) And here is the other one. (beat) (dry) The egg you asked for, in 1991, on a Monday, at eleven o'clock at night, off the menu, which I said no to, and which I have thought about every single Tuesday for nine years, and which I did not have a name for until a woman in a warm chair wrote it on a ticket and put it in a coat. (quieter) It is not on the menu. (beat) (dry) I put it on the wall in chalk, in small print, because Phoebe is a better writer than I am and because I wanted you to have to lean in for it. (quieter) (wiping my hands on the towel, not looking up) Eat. (beat) (dry) And then we will talk about the bread, because that is what we are going to talk about tonight, and I have thought about it for nine years and it is a wonderful subject and there is absolutely nothing else I would rather discuss. (quieter) (quietly, to nobody) It is a dollar. It was always a dollar.
S05/E01.md:387:Phoebe: (Tuesday, eleven twenty, the corner) Okay, Ross, I am going to say her name out loud, because the song does not have a chair in it. (beat) (dry) It has a person in it. (quieter) Estelle. (dry) I have said it badly, and the second time is going to be better. (quieter) The second time is when she answers.
S05/E01.md:435:Joey: (Tuesday, eleven twenty-three, standing up, not sitting down, my hand on the back of my own chair) Okay, Estelle, I am going to ask you the one question, because I am the man who read it out loud and I have to live in this building. (beat) (dry) You came six Mondays. Then you stopped. (quieter) What happened on the seventh? (beat) (dry) Because I set that plate every week for six years, and I would really like to know what I was waiting for.
S05/E01.md:453:Chandler: (Tuesday, eleven twenty-four, the table, a glass of water in the air) Okay, Phoebe. Phoebe. (beat) (dry) And since nobody has said a name at this table in nine years, I am going to do a toast. (quieter) Ross, Rachel, Monica, Joey, Phoebe, and Estelle. (beat) (dry) Say it with me. (quieter) It is not a bit, it is a job.
S05/E01.md:465:Joey: (Tuesday, eleven twenty-five, the table, my water glass up, the heel of the loaf in my other hand) Okay, Chandler, a toast, I am in, I have never turned down a toast in my life. (beat) (dry) Ross, Rachel, Monica, Joey, Phoebe, and Estelle. (beat) (dry) And I would like it noted that I am the only man here who has said her name out loud before, so this is a nice moment for me. (quieter) (handing her the heel) And this is the good part.
S05/E01.md:513:Joey: (Tuesday, eleven twenty-nine, the table, my chair pushed in, watching the seventh plate) Okay, everybody, I have been looking at that plate for two minutes and the sandwich is not moving and the egg is not moving. (beat) (dry) Do not everybody look at it at once, that is worse. (quieter) Estelle, take your time, but that thing is still hot, and if it stops being hot that is my fault, because I brought the oven in on a truck with the hazards on. (dry) So eat it hot. That is the one instruction I have got.
S05/E01.md:549:Rachel: (Tuesday, eleven thirty, the table, the plate in front of the seventh place) Okay. (beat) (dry) I have been rehearsing that since nine fifty and everybody saw, so I will not pretend it is spontaneous. (quieter) Estelle. (beat) (dry) That is your name, and it has been in my coat for six years, and I am sorry I said it to a plate instead of your face.

content.thinking:
Rich backstory. Estelle = the woman who wrote "Table for seven" in 1991. Chandler (the "C") ate standing up. The "seventh chair" man "never once sat down" (S05/E08: "a man who never once sat down turns around"). Wait — in E08, "a man who never once sat down turns around to give her the sandwich he has been keeping warm" — that's Chandler? Hmm, E07 says "finds Chandler instead". So the letter C = Chandler, who ate standing up.

Then in E15, the stranger in the wet coat arrives and takes the seventh chair, ordering black no sugar like Estelle. Now E16: Monica discovered the wall line was her own handwriting (she invented the order), the seventh chair was just the best seat, coffee rings from whoever wanted it. So the ghost-woman premise dissolves into: they invented Estelle partly, but Estelle was real (she wrote the ticket). There's ambiguity: Monica said "I invented her" (1997 chalk line). Hmm.

Now the stranger in the wet coat: four years of Mondays, black no sugar, name on a ticket in Monica's drawer in her handwriting. So Monica knew his name for four years and never wrote a name down before or after.

So who is the stranger? Perhaps the man in the wet coat is the "C"?? No, C = Chandler. Perhaps he's "Ernie" — the guy who came to the restaurant for 19 years (S05/E03: "a guest of nineteen years orders one dollar of her own"). Hmm.

I'm free to name him. But careful: if Ross writes the name in his next commit, and it differs from mine, the transcript has a contradiction. I'll name him and tell Ross to write exactly it: "Ray." Hmm, or maybe better to have the name already known by Monica on the ticket — she says she knows his name. So the name exists in-story on a ticket in a drawer in Monica's handwriting. Since Monica wrote it, it should be a plain name. "Ernie" is warm and plain; also "Ernie" is a name from a seat in a theatre... Let me choose "Ray". Hmm, "Ray" could evoke "Ray's" ... fine.

Alternatively, avoid the risk: have Rachel say the name and explicitly tell Ross to write it down exactly. If Ross writes a different name, the story would be inconsistent — Ross would have read my commit, so he'd use my name. Low risk. Good.

Now, should the name be said out loud in the room? Phoebe's latest line says nobody will say it out loud. To respect that, Rachel says the name to Ross only — but for the transcript's payoff it's nicer if the reader learns it. Compromise: Rachel says it once, out loud, and immediately says "and nobody says it again, and if I hear it at this table again I'm changing the subject" — i.e., she says it exactly once, satisfying "a name you say twice is a name you have started talking about." Phoebe's line said nobody would say it out loud — but Phoebe also said "He said it, and Ross wrote it" — implying it's already done in her telling. So it's roughly consistent that the name exists but isn't repeated. If Rachel says it once, it contradicts "nobody is going to say it out loud" slightly, but Rachel could frame it as: "I am saying it once, because I asked it and it deserves to exist in a room, and then nobody says it again."

Hmm, alternatively Rachel asks him to write it on a napkin — "because some names are better written than said" — and she hands the napkin to Ross. Then the transcript never shows the name. That's a bit unsatisfying but thematically consistent with the room's rules and with the epic's tendency to withhold (the name out loud is a big motif — E09 "The One With the Name Out Loud").

Actually here's a strong idea: The name is the payoff, but it can be delivered by Rachel out loud exactly once, and the room goes quiet — mirroring E09 when the name was said out loud. That's a nice callback: "Nobody in this room has said a name out loud at a table in nine years, and I am about to do it once."

Wait — E09 says six people say a name out loud at once. So names have been said. Phoebe's current line is about not repeating a name twice (gossip). Fine: Rachel says it once, and says it directly to the man and the room, and asks that it not be repeated. Good enough, with a self-aware joke.

Now the second question: "What do you want?" — Rachel asks it (Phoebe's second line). The man says something other than his habit.

Also, an important dramatic beat: the man in the wet coat has been eating free off an invented chair for four years; Monica says the seventh place costs a dollar; Joey cut the sandwich for him. Now the scene should close S05/E16 with something that opens the next episode — but Ross opens episodes.

Also Rachel's personal arc: "finding independence".
